name: Do Nothing meditation
origin: Named and taught by American meditation teacher Shinzen Young, who describes it in his free manual Five Ways to Know Yourself (versions from about 2011) and in his later ULTRA system, and who links it to older practices such as Zen 'just sitting' and Tibetan Dzogchen and Mahamudra.
summary: Do Nothing is a meditation with no object and a single instruction: let whatever happens happen, and whenever you notice an intention to control your attention, drop it. Even mind wandering is not corrected, since steering attention back would itself be a form of control. It sits at the effortless, receptive end of meditation, in contrast to methods that train focus or build up a feeling.
theoryOfChange: Most meditation builds skill through effort, such as holding attention on an object; Do Nothing trains the opposite skill of letting go of control, which Jeff Warren, a teacher of the method, calls a training in equanimity (staying even-minded with whatever comes). Young writes that when the intention to focus is dropped, a focused state tends to arise on its own over time, which is why he says it could also be called Auto Focus. Mindfulness research suggests this hands-off, accepting attitude matters: Lindsay and Creswell's Monitor and Acceptance Theory proposes that awareness training alone can heighten emotional reactions, and that acceptance is what turns awareness into lower stress.
whatYouDo: You sit comfortably, eyes open or closed, without choosing anything to focus on. Thoughts, sounds, body feelings and daydreams are all allowed to come and go. Whenever you notice an intention to control your attention, such as trying to focus, to fix a feeling or to meditate well, you let that intention go; if there is no such intention, there is nothing to do.
typicalDose: Sitting practice, guided or alone, often 10 to 30 minutes, daily or a few times a week; Jeff Warren's live Do Nothing Project broadcasts include a 25-minute guided sit. There is no fixed course: it is usually one technique within a broader mindfulness practice and can also be used on retreat.
keyTechniques: Drop any intention to control attention
Allow mind wandering instead of correcting it
Let focus arise by itself (Auto Focus)

evidence.summary: No controlled studies of the Do Nothing technique on its own were found, so its support is theory and practitioner accounts. The nearest research looks at open monitoring meditation, where attention rests on whatever arises instead of a chosen object (Lutz and colleagues, 2008), and at acceptance as an active ingredient of mindfulness (Lindsay and Creswell, 2017). In a 2019 randomized trial of 153 stressed adults, co-authored by Young, a 14-lesson app built on his Unified Mindfulness system cut daily loneliness by about 22 percent when it trained both monitoring and acceptance, while monitoring alone did not; that program covered much more than Do Nothing, so the link is indirect.

goodFitFor: People who find meditation effortful or strained, experienced meditators who want to rest in open awareness, and people who dislike detailed instructions.
cautions: With no anchor, beginners may drift, doze or slide into worry, which is one reason it is usually taught alongside more focused techniques. Like any meditation, open sitting can bring up difficult emotions or memories; it is not a treatment for mental illness, and people with severe depression, trauma, psychosis or dissociation should practice with a qualified teacher and talk to a clinician.
namingNote: 'Do Nothing' is Shinzen Young's name for this technique (he notes it could also be called Auto Focus), and teachers such as Jeff Warren teach it under the same name. Young and others compare it to Zen shikantaza ('just sitting'), Tibetan Dzogchen and Mahamudra, and choiceless awareness, and Kagyu Mahamudra teaching gives a close instruction: no distraction, no control, no work. Those traditions have their own views and methods, so this point means the Young-style technique. It is kept apart from Vipassana, which actively observes and labels experience, and from Metta / Jhana, which deliberately builds a feeling and deep concentration.
